Today, when no billing choice is saved, reviews by members who have a paid Copilot license use the member’s Copilot entitlement. Starting December 30, 2026, those reviews will be billed to the organization that owns the repository. Accounts that don’t have AI Credits paid usage enabled, have a billing lock, or have no billable customer will be set to Member instead. If you already chose Member or Organization , your choice stays in effect. The separate setting for members without a Copilot license doesn’t change.

entries.titleEn: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
entries.summaryJa: このエントリは github-copilot から収集した copilot 領域の最新アップデートです。原題:「How to choose the next safe step in application modernization」。AI による日本語要約は次回以降の Worker run で生成されます。
entries.summaryEn: How to choose the next safe step in application modernization
entries.contentSnippet: A request to modernize an application often starts with a technology question: Which framework should replace the old one? Before you choose, find out what still works. Then collect evidence that can act as a regression net for that behavior and show where modernization is necessary. I used an evidence-first method on four public applications, from a small Node.js game to a large Java enterprise resource planning (ERP) application. Each needed a different treatment, but the way I collected evidence, chose the next experiment, and decided on possible proof points was repeatable. This post walks through that process so you can apply it to one application of your own. It also shows how to encode the procedure in a GitHub Copilot agent skill while keeping architectural judgment with the people responsible for the system. The label on an application rarely tells you enough.
entries.feedSnippet: Learn how to assess a legacy application, choose a bounded modernization step, and reuse the method with a GitHub Copilot agent skill. The post How to choose the next safe step in application modernization appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

entries.title: More predictable notifications on GitHub.com
entries.titleEn: More predictable notifications on GitHub.com
entries.contentSnippet: Starting December 1, 2026, we’re migrating notifications on GitHub.com over the course of a week to make subscriptions more predictable, correct unexpected behavior, and support the growing scale of activity. During the rollout, notifications may behave differently for different users. No action is required, but the changes below may affect how you manage and filter notifications. This does not apply to GitHub Enterprise Server. Routine activity won’t resubscribe you: Previously, after manually unsubscribing, notification activities such as commenting, submitting a pull request review, changing a thread’s state, or merge queue activity resulted in a re-subscription. Now, those actions leave you unsubscribed. Being mentioned, assigned, or receiving a pull request review request will continue to resubscribe you since those actions ask for your attention.

entries.title: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
entries.titleEn: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval
entries.contentSnippet: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval A guide to the new managed ingestion and SearchDocuments features in Agent Retrieval , for searching PDFs, Office files, and videos without writing an ingestion pipeline. Before an agent can answer a question about your PDFs, someone has to build the pipeline: parse every file, split it into chunks, embed each chunk, write the chunks to a vector database, and then learn that database's schema to query it. For video it gets harder: transcode the files, cut them into clips, embed the frames, and keep track of which second of which video each clip came from. Before: every step of the pipeline is custom code you write and maintain, separately for documents and for videos. Most of that code has nothing to do with your application.
entries.feedSnippet: Agent Retrieval in Vertex AI introduces managed ingestion and SearchDocuments to replace custom chunking and embedding pipelines. Developers can now import document and video files directly from Cloud Storage and query them with a single API call for cited page numbers and timestamped results. The feature supports hybrid retrieval, metadata filtering, reranking, and multimodal video audio search.

image.alt: From Files to Cited Answers in One API Call: Managed Ingestion and SearchDocuments in Agent Retrieval

entries.contentSnippet: GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer GLM 5.4 is now available from Chinese AI lab Z.ai. It's their first model to use a looped transformer architecture, which they describe like this: In a standard Transformer, each layer runs once per forward pass. In a Loop Transformer, a group of weight-shared layers runs for multiple iterations, refining the hidden states from the previous pass. This gives us a deeper network without increasing the parameter count. This is the second mention of looped transformers I've seen in the past week - the first was Inkling 2 Mini from Thinking Machines Lab on November 20th, who said: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer, running the middle layers of the model three times for every token. entries.titleEn: Issue statuses and repository boards are in public preview
entries.contentSnippet: Open or closed doesn’t always tell you where an issue stands. You can now use more specific statuses to give your team and agents shared context about what’s in flight and what to work on next, then visualize your progress with repository boards. Track progress directly on an issue. Choose a status when creating an issue or change it from the issue header. You’ll see it reflected in issue icons across the repository issues page, the issues dashboard , and repository boards, where you can use the status: filter to find the issues you’re looking for. Automated status updates. To help keep your statuses accurate, the following automations are applied to your issues: Linking a draft pull request to an issue moves the issue to In progress . Marking a draft pull request as Ready for review moves the issue to In review . Linking an open pull request to an issue moves the issue to In review .

entries.title: Code coverage uploads now flag invalid report formats
entries.titleEn: Code coverage uploads now flag invalid report formats
entries.contentSnippet: The GitHub Code Quality upload-code-coverage action now checks that your coverage report is in Cobertura XML format. If it isn’t in a supported format, the upload step fails and the Actions log shows this error: This file is not a Cobertura XML report. Upload a Cobertura XML report. Previously, these uploads appeared to succeed, but no coverage showed up on your pull requests. Now you’ll find out about the problem in the workflow run, with a clear next step. If your workflow begins failing with this error, configure your test framework to output Cobertura XML, or convert your report to Cobertura XML before the upload step. We’ve also made processing more forgiving for valid Cobertura reports. We no longer reject a report because of minor structural issues, and we skip individual lines that don’t have a usable line number or hit count instead of discarding the whole report.

This change applies to the detailed usage report, the AI usage report, and the premium request usage report, including exports you create with the GitHub REST API. The summarized usage report won’t change. These changes apply to all GitHub Enterprise Cloud account types and standalone organizations on GitHub Team. If your scripts or tools read these reports by column position, update them to read columns by header name before December 1. entries.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
entries.titleEn: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
entries.contentSnippet: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

entries.title: Security advisory permissions are now generally available
entries.titleEn: Security advisory permissions are now generally available
entries.contentSnippet: Organization owners can now let people work on repository security advisories, including private vulnerability reports, through custom repository roles . You no longer have to make them repository administrators or give them the organization-wide security manager role. Four new permissions are available under Security when you create or edit a custom repository role: View security advisories : view draft security advisories, their status, and comments. Create, Edit, and Manage security advisories : everything in View, plus Create and Edit advisories, comment, manage collaborators, and create a temporary private fork. Accept private vulnerability reports and close or reopen security advisories : requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage . Publish security advisories and request CVEs : requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage .

entries.titleEn: GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host
entries.contentSnippet: GitHub Desktop now lets you sign in with more than one account on the same host, including GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GHE.com. This has been one of the most requested features in the Desktop community. Add more than one account for a single host, with no fixed limit. Associate each repository with a specific account, so clone, publish, and Git operations use the right credentials automatically. Choose an account when adding or cloning a repository that multiple signed-in accounts can access, or let Desktop infer it when only one can. Change a repository’s account association at any time from repository settings or the repository list’s context menu. Existing repositories are migrated automatically to the account you were already using, so if you only have one account per host, nothing changes for you.

entries.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
entries.titleEn: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
entries.contentSnippet: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies Two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who says they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language. Permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules.
entries.feedSnippet: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

entries.title: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
entries.titleEn: How to securely connect internal Cloud Run MCP servers to Gemini Enterprise
entries.contentSnippet: Enterprise teams adopting Gemini Enterprise are increasingly building custom Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to connect AI agents with internal APIs, databases, and business workflows. Google Cloud Run is a natural fit for hosting these lightweight StreamableHTTP MCP servers: it scales automatically, manages TLS certificates out of the box, and integrates natively with Cloud IAM. However, moving a custom MCP server from an initial prototype to an enterprise production environment immediately introduces three real-world security and networking challenges: No public internet exposure (internal-only ingress): Enterprise security policies require internal MCP servers to block all public internet traffic and accept requests only from private Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) networks.
entries.feedSnippet: How to connect Gemini Enterprise privately to internal StreamableHTTP MCP servers on Cloud Run using Egress Agent Gateway, Private Service Connect, FQDN-scoped Private Cloud DNS, and dual-header OAuth 2.0 authentication.

entries.title: Can AI help build a healthier future?
entries.titleEn: Can AI help build a healthier future?
entries.contentSnippet: Technical advancement is moving at such a rapid pace that it can be challenging to define the tomorrow we’re working toward. In The Shape of Things to Come , Microsoft Research leader Doug Burger and experts from across disciplines tease out the thorniest AI issues facing technologists, policymakers, business decisionmakers, and other stakeholders today. The goal: to amplify the shared understanding needed to build a future in which the AI transition is a net positive. Microsoft Principal Research Manager Ava Amini , Microsoft Chief Scientific Officer Eric Horvitz , and physician-scientist and Microsoft AI health advisor Eric Topol (opens in new tab) of Scripps Research join Burger to tackle a question with ramifications for every individual on the planet: What might the future of medicine look like with AI, and what needs to happen first?

entries.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
entries.titleEn: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
entries.contentSnippet: Developers use AI coding agents in the same codebases day after day, yet agents often start each session from scratch: rediscovering familiar facts, loading unused tools, and repeating unsuccessful approaches. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that learns from an agent’s past sessions in a repository to reduce waste in future sessions, without modifying the agent or its underlying model. Across 277 real bug-fixing tasks, TokenEconomizer reduced costs by 18.4–30.9% across multiple AI coding agents. Costs fell in every repository tested, while task success rates remained broadly stable. AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model.
entries.feedSnippet: AI coding agents can waste time and tokens relearning the same lessons. TokenEconomizer is an open-source plugin that builds on past sessions to cut costs while maintaining task success. It’s a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. The post TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient appeared first on Microsoft Research .

entries.summaryEn: Cuttlefish on Mac: Running Android’s Virtual Device Framework Natively on Apple Silicon
entries.contentSnippet: How Meta's Reality Labs brought Cuttlefish and its QEMU backend to macOS and Apple silicon. Meta’s Reality Labs builds products such as AI glasses . Emulators provide us with a way to scale development and testing without relying on scarce physical hardware. Testing software for non-phone Android devices depends on how closely a virtual device reproduces the software behavior of the physical product. While a lightweight emulator like Goldfish gets you part of the way, differences from the real device can hide bugs until later in development. This lack of fidelity also erodes trust in device emulation, increasing reliance on scarce physical hardware. Cuttlefish is the Android Open Source Project’s (AOSP’s) virtual-device framework for testing Android software against virtual hardware.

entries.summaryEn: Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills
entries.contentSnippet: How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline. An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.
entries.feedSnippet: Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them. The post Build once, run on any agent: A practical guide to agent skills appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

entries.contentSnippet: By Zhaojun Zhang , Qinwei Zhu , Gang Li , Jianwei Xiao , Yanan Wang , Hongmei Li , Deepak Vijaywargi , Ke Pan , Li Yu Ads ranking models are growing toward LLM scale faster than the hardware to run them can keep up. An extra unit of compute has more impact on some ad requests, models, and chips than on others. The challenge is deciding where to allocate it to get the best outcome for the entire system. We built Intelligent Delivery, an ML-driven system that allocates resources across the serving stack toward the system-wide optimum. It has delivered ~10% incremental ranking performance on top of model and system advancements since 2017.

entries.summaryEn: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
entries.contentSnippet: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe.
entries.feedSnippet: Writing code got faster. The work around it didn't. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment. The post Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering appeared first on The GitHub Blog .

entries.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
entries.titleEn: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
entries.contentSnippet: AI agents can generate code at a scale that’s hard for humans to review line-by-line. PDD Kit helps ensure the code is doing what the developer intended by creating formal specifications and testing against them. It converts developer intent into a Verus specification, proves AI-generated code meets it for every input, and uses tests where proofs aren't practical. Developers review intent, not every line. The post Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit appeared first on Microsoft Research .
